title: Pennsylvania Measles Outbreak Tops 1,000 Cases, Largest in US in Three Decades
excerpt: State health officials confirmed 1,004 cases as of Oct. 5, with 198 hospitalizations and five deaths — all in unvaccinated people — as the US endures its worst measles year since 1991.
body:
• Pennsylvania has confirmed 1,004 measles cases this year, state health officials said Monday — the largest outbreak in a single US state in more than three decades. The outbreak began in April west of Philadelphia, with 106 new cases in the past week alone.
  • The toll includes 198 hospitalizations and five deaths, all in unvaccinated people. Lancaster County, home to large Amish and Mennonite communities, remains the hardest hit with 391 cases; more than 99% of all cases statewide were in people not fully vaccinated.
  • The milestone comes as the US endures its worst measles year since 1991, with the CDC recording 3,887 cases across 47 states — and as New York declared a disaster emergency over its own rural outbreak of 108 cases.
  • What it means for you: the MMR vaccine is 97% effective after two doses — check your family's vaccination records, especially before international travel. Measles lingers in the air for up to two hours, and up to 9 in 10 susceptible people exposed to it get infected, according to the CDC. If you are unvaccinated and may have been exposed, contact a healthcare provider promptly.

Pennsylvania has surpassed 1,000 measles cases this year, state health officials said Monday, making it the largest outbreak in a single American state in more than three decades — and the grimmest marker yet of the country's worst measles year since 1991.

The state health department reported 1,004 confirmed cases as of Oct. 5, with 106 new cases counted in the past seven days. The outbreak, which began in April in communities west of Philadelphia, has produced 198 hospitalizations and five deaths. All five people who died were unvaccinated, according to state officials.

The epicenter: Lancaster County

Lancaster County remains the hardest-hit area with 391 confirmed cases, followed by Mifflin County with 118 and Chester County with 84. Cases have been confirmed across 39 counties. Health officials say the outbreak has been driven by low vaccination rates in under-immunized communities, including large Amish and Mennonite populations in Lancaster County — a pattern mirrored in Ohio, which shares a border with Pennsylvania and has logged more than 200 cases this year, some in counties with large Amish communities.

https://x.com/WGNNews/status/2107411039642112260

The demographics underscore the vaccine gap. More than 99% of Pennsylvania's confirmed cases occurred in people who were not fully vaccinated. About 32% of infections were in people under 18, and 18% of those pediatric patients required hospitalization. The fifth measles-associated death was reported Sept. 30 in Lancaster County.

"I would bet that this goes on for at least another three to six months. We have seen an increase in vaccinations, but we aren't seeing enough people get vaccinated to stop the epidemic."

— Dr. John Goldman, infectious disease expert at the University of Pittsburgh Medical Center

A national resurgence

Pennsylvania is the leading edge of a national crisis. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has recorded 3,887 measles cases in 2026 so far — the most since the major resurgence between 1989 and 1991, when 55,000 infections and 123 deaths were recorded. Forty-two separate outbreaks have been documented this year, representing about 95% of all reported infections, and roughly 95% of cases occurred in unvaccinated people.

The death toll is drawing scrutiny. Eight measles-associated deaths have been reported nationwide in the past two years — more than the combined total of the previous three decades. Pennsylvania is the only state to report measles-associated deaths this year, yet the CDC's website has so far officially acknowledged only two deaths nationally, without naming the states. The agency says it is working with state epidemiologists on a standard definition for measles-related deaths.

Other states are also struggling. Three states have reported more than 500 cases this year: Pennsylvania, South Carolina (997) and Utah. Texas and Ohio are dealing with significant outbreaks of their own.

New York's emergency and the road ahead

On Monday, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul declared a state disaster emergency over growing measles cases — a story The Videshi covered on Oct. 6. New York has logged 108 cases this year, 92 of them since July 15 among under-immunized rural communities across 18 counties. The executive order deputizes paramedics, pharmacists, certified midwives and other health professionals to administer the MMR vaccine, and allows nurses to order measles testing. Local health departments have already administered more than 1,000 MMR doses in the affected communities.

"No one should get seriously ill or die from a vaccine-preventable disease."

— Gov. Kathy Hochul, announcing New York's disaster emergency

The stakes extend beyond this year's case counts. The US eliminated domestic measles spread in 2000 by maintaining high vaccination rates, but coverage has fallen below the 95% threshold needed to prevent outbreaks. In November, international health officials will meet to determine whether the US and Mexico have lost their measles-free status — more than a quarter century after the disease was declared locally eliminated. Johns Hopkins University's independent tally has already put nationwide infections above 4,000.

For diaspora families traveling between the US and India, the outbreak is a practical reminder: measles spreads through coughing and sneezing, survives on surfaces, and lingers in the air for up to two hours — including in airports and on planes. Checking MMR records before flying protects both the traveler and the communities on either end of the journey.
